content: The public domain refers to a collection of knowledge and creative works, such as literature, art, music, and inventions, that are not subject to proprietary rights within a specific legal jurisdiction. This means no individual or legal entity can claim ownership or exclusive rights over these works. Works in the public domain are considered part of a shared cultural and intellectual heritage. They can generally be used or exploited by anyone for both commercial and non-commercial purposes without legal restrictions. Approximately 15% of all books are in the public domain, including 10% of books that are still in print. If a work is not in the public domain, it is likely protected by proprietary rights such as copyright, patents, or other sui generis rights. The extent to which the public can use or exploit such works is determined by the scope of these proprietary rights within the relevant legal jurisdiction. When copyrights, patents, or other proprietary restrictions expire, the work enters the public domain and becomes freely available for use by anyone for any purpose. A creative work is considered to be in the public domain if there are no laws restricting its use by the general public. For example, a work may enter the public domain if no laws establish proprietary rights over it, or if the work or its subject matter is explicitly excluded from existing legal protections. Since proprietary rights are governed by national laws, a work may be in the public domain in one jurisdiction but not in another. For instance, some literary works are in the public domain in the United States but remain protected in the European Union, and vice versa. The underlying ideas expressed in a work are generally not subject to copyright protection. For example, mathematical formulas are typically part of the public domain unless their specific expression, such as in software, is protected by copyright. However, algorithms may be patentable in certain jurisdictions. Works created before the establishment of copyright and patent laws are also part of the public domain. Examples include the Bible and the inventions of Archimedes. However, translations or new adaptations of these works may still be protected by copyright. While intellectual property laws are not designed to prevent facts from entering the public domain, collections of facts organized or presented in a creative manner, such as categorized lists, may be copyrighted. For example, alphabetized directories like telephone books are generally not copyrightable, but their unique organization or layout may be. In some countries, copyright-like protections are granted for databases, even those containing mere facts. The European Union, for instance, has a sui generis database rights regime. Works created by the United States government are automatically in the public domain upon creation. Examples include military journalism, federal court opinions, congressional reports, and census data. However, works created by contractors for the government may still be subject to copyright. Even public domain documents may have their availability restricted by laws governing the dissemination of classified information. Before 1978, unpublished works in the United States were protected under perpetual common law copyright. The Copyright Act of 1976, effective in 1978, abolished common law copyright, bringing all works, whether published or unpublished, under federal statutory copyright. The claim that pre-1923 works are in the public domain is accurate only for published works. Unpublished works remain under federal copyright for at least the life of the author plus 70 years. For works made for hire, copyright in works created before 1978 but not previously in the public domain or registered for copyright lasts for 95 years from the year of first publication or 120 years from the year of creation, whichever expires first. Sound recordings fixed before February 15, 1972, were generally covered by common law or state statutes rather than federal copyright law. The 1976 Copyright Act provided federal copyright protection for sound recordings fixed on or after February 15, 1972. Recordings fixed before this date remain protected under state laws until February 15, 2067. Critics of copyright term extensions argue that Congress has effectively created perpetual copyright terms through incremental extensions. In British law, government works are subject to Crown Copyright or Parliamentary Copyright. Published Crown Copyright works enter the public domain 50 years after publication unless the author assigned copyright to the Crown, in which case the term is the life of the author plus 70 years. Unpublished Crown Copyright documents enter the public domain 125 years after creation. In Canada and New Zealand, copyright terms are generally the life of the author plus 50 years. Australia extended its copyright term by 20 years in 2004, but this extension did not revive already-expired copyrights. In Thailand, the copyright term is the life of the author plus 50 years. For works by legal entities or anonymous authors, the term is 50 years from publication. Thai state documents are in the public domain. Japanese copyright law does not explicitly mention the public domain. As a result, even materials considered in the public domain may have use restrictions. The term copyright-free is sometimes used instead. Examples of inventions whose patents have expired include those of Thomas Edison. Examples of works whose copyrights have expired include the works of Carlo Collodi, Mozart, and most of Mark Twain's works, except for those first published posthumously. In the United States, works created by government agencies are public domain at the moment of creation. However, works created by contractors for the government may still be copyrighted. Laws may render certain types of works and inventions ineligible for proprietary rights, causing them to enter the public domain immediately upon publication. For example, abstract ideas like Charles Darwin's theory of evolution are not patentable. In the past, works in the United States would enter the public domain if released without a copyright notice. This was true before March 1, 1989, but is no longer the case. Today, any work fixed in a tangible medium automatically receives copyright protection. While copyright law does not provide a statutory mechanism to abandon copyright and place a work in the public domain, it is possible to do so through common law principles. Statutory law includes references to placing copyrighted works into the public domain. For example, the Computer Software Rental Amendments Act of 1990 allows for the recordation of public domain shareware with the Library of Congress. Judicial rulings, such as the case of Computer Associates Int'l v. Altai, have established that material in the public domain cannot be appropriated by a single author, even if included in a copyrighted work.
